newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban accepts north leader's talks offer.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban accepts north leader's talks offer.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia on Monday accepted an offer of peace talks by northern leader General Abdul Malik, but demanded that he demonstrate his sincerity by releasing prisoners-of-war.

A Taleban spokesman's statement was quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service a day after Malik said in the northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif that he was willing to negotiate with the the fundamentalist militia and asked Afghanistan's neighbours to mediate.

"We are prepared for talks with General Malik," the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted spokesman Wakil Ahmad as saying by telephone from the southern Afghan city of Kandahar, the headquarters of the Taleban movement.
"But to show his sincerity, he should release our prisoners who are being held illegally," he said.

The remarks seemed somewhat softer than previous Taleban statements that had cited prisoners' release as a pre-condition for any dialogue with Malik, whose forces drove the militia from Mazar-i-Sharif on May 28, four days after helping to take it.

But Ahmad rejected a proposal by an official of the Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction, a Malik ally, to turn Afghanistan into a federated state split into four provinces, saying Taleban wanted strong central government.
He said Taleban officials and fighters had gone to Mazar-i-Sharif at Malik's invitation and it was immoral to make them prisoners.
Malik told reporters in Mazar-i-Sharif on Sunday that the Taleban must share power to bring peace to Afghanistan.

Three weeks ago, Malik switched sides as an opposition commander to defect to the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, and with its help, drove then opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum from Mazar-i-Sharif.
Three days later, he turned on his new allies and, after fierce battles that cost at least 300 dead, forced them to flee with the help of Hezb-i-Wahdat.
Both Taleban and Malik accuse each other of breaking an agreement between the two sides and starting the clashes.
Malik said on Sunday about 10,000 Taleban prisoners had been taken in the north, but other Afghan sources say the number may be much less.

The prisoners include the Taleban government's Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous, northern commander Mullah Abdul Razzaq and central bank chief Mullah Ahsanullah, who were in Mazar-i-Sharif at the time of the fighting.
"If the Taleban persist in fighting, the lives of the prisoners will be in danger and the responsibility will rest with them," Malik said.
However, he said the Taleban should not let their losses in the north stand in the way of rapprochement and called for forgiveness from both sides.
